title: Throughput stochasticity: quant fingerprint field diary
content:
Purpose and context
This is a running field diary of observations from a cluster of small experiments run between Sep–Nov 2023 to investigate surprising throughput stochasticity when serving quantized model variants (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) on the usual GPU fleet. The problem: two seemingly-identical model variants and kernel combinations produce stable mean throughput but wildly different tail behaviour and intermittent 10–30% drops in observed tokens/sec under light–moderate load. We suspect interaction between kernel selection, microburst arrival patterns, and KV-cache/batchshape transitions.

High-level hypothesis
1) A small proportion of requests follow code paths that trigger a less-optimized kernel (tiling/memory layout) which increases stalls and reduces throughput for a short window (2–20s).
2) Kernel switching and scheduler backpressure produce congestion waves that amplify when quantization changes memory footprint or instruction mix (e.g., AWQ reduces memory reads but increases integer ops).
3) Real-world prefix reuse (KV cache hits) interacts with batching in a way synthetic steady-state tests miss.

Quick summary of experiments run
- Microburst replay: replayed 30s bursts derived from a recorded customer workload (mixed short + long contexts) at 2x peak QPS while toggling model variant and kernel.
- Stochastic seed sweep: repeated the same replay with 20 different random seeds for request ordering and found run-to-run variance up to 28% in 95th percentile throughput on AWQ kernels.
- KV warm/cold alternation: toggled sequences to create alternating cold KV and warm KV requests to surface batching mismatch.
- Thread offload toggles: switched between CUDA kernel-sync and host-queue driven dispatch to see scheduler sensitivity.

Representative findings (notes, not polished stats)
- Pattern A (short-heavy bursts): INT8 + kernel-X produced consistent high throughput but occasional ~12% drops during bursts. The drops correlated with a rise in device memory copies visible in perf counters.
- Pattern B (longer contexts with high KV hits): AWQ + kernel-Y performed worse on tail throughput, despite similar median. The likely cause: kernel-Y uses an algorithmic path that is friendly to dense matmuls but has higher register pressure when sequence length grows, causing more frequent fallback paths and spilling.
- Seed dependence: different ordering of request lengths within a burst changed batch shapes sufficiently to flip which kernel the scheduler chose; one ordering kept using kernel-X, another ordering forced kernel-Y -> large tail difference.
- Scheduler hysteresis: our kernel-router appears to have a short cooldown window before it will re-evaluate a switch. When a bad ordering triggers kernel-Y, the router stays on it for several hundred milliseconds and that amplified the transient.

Profiling knobs and telemetry used
- GPU metrics: nvprof/perf counters for L2 cache misses, DRAM bytes, sm_efficiency, achieved_occupancy.
- Runtime traces: serveflow traces with per-request kernel decision logs, queue lengths, and batchshape snapshots.
- Microsecond timeline: linux perf + CUPTI sampled stack traces during the drop windows.
- Synthetic timers: gperf-based timers inserted around dispatch and kernel launch to measure enqueue-to-complete latency.

Concrete example trace (simplified)
- t=0: burst start, QPS spikes -> batches form with mixed seq lengths (8, 64, 512). Kernel selector probes predicted cost and picks kernel-X (low latency).
- t=3s: a run of long-context requests arrives; batchshape shifts to longer sequences; selector picks kernel-Y (higher throughput for long contexts).
- t=3.2s: kernel-Y exhibits higher register pressure -> SM stalls -> DRAM reads increase -> device-to-host copies spike (we think due to occasional fallback shared-memory sync path).
- t=3.9s: queue depth increases, subsequent short requests are forced onto kernel-Y because router cooldown prevents immediate switch. Throughput drops until queue drains (t ~ 6.3s).

What made this different from steady-state bench results
- Steady-state benches use repeated fixed-length requests and remove KV cache variability; they therefore lock in a single kernel path and miss transition costs.
- Real traffic creates a distribution of batchshapes; the selector’s cost function is approximate and sometimes mispredicts at runtime.

Ideas for quant fingerprinting (how to detect vulnerable model+kernel combos)
- Fingerprint vector: {median_throughput, p95_throughput, swap_count, kernel_switch_rate, avg_batchshape_entropy, kv_hit_ratio, sm_efficiency_var}. Compute via short 60s bursts with representative length distribution to produce a low-cost fingerprint.
- Fault signatures: high kernel_switch_rate + batchshape_entropy correlates strongly with tail drops.
- Synthetic probe: inject pseudo-random long-context spike in a small percentage of traffic and measure responsiveness. If tail falls by >10%, mark as high-risk.

Quick mitigations to try (low-effort first)
- Reduce router cooldown: shorten the period before re-evaluating kernel choice to allow quicker recovery back to efficient kernels after short spikes. Risk: thrash-flipping.
- Batchshape-aware sticky routing: allow selector to remember recent batchshape distribution and prefer kernels that were successful in the last N seconds for similar batch profiles.
- Pre-emptive warmup: upon seeing a long-context request, pre-warm long-context kernel on a shadow stream so first few long requests use warmed kernel.
- KV-awareness: include KV-hit ratio as an explicit input to the cost model.

Longer term / research directions
- Learning-based selector: train a lightweight online model to predict expected latency for each kernel given the recent request distribution, and add a loss term for avoiding tail amplifications.
- Kernel-level microprofiling: instrument kernels to emit lightweight histograms of register spilling and shared-memory thrash to make the cause less fuzzy.
- Admission control: if a fingerprint indicates a particular model+kernel combo is high-risk under bursty traffic, route it to a more conservative variant (e.g., slightly higher-precision kernel or a quantization profile with less aggressive packing).

Action items and follow-ups
- Diego: roll a short experiment with router cooldown at 50% of current and re-run the original microburst replay (JIRA:RUNTIME-2314). Target by 2024-01-22.
- Aisha: implement fingerprint probe harness (60s burst runner + metric extractor) and add to bench registry. Draft PR: GH:repo/infra/profiler#412. Target by 2024-01-19.
- Priya: collect more traces from customer-like traffic and produce fingerprint vectors for 6 models (LLM-small, LLM-base, LLM-chat variants) by next week.

Open questions / unknowns
- Are we seeing any hardware-specific idiosyncrasies (arch A vs arch B) that make certain kernels more fragile? Need to run same experiments across both Tesla and Ampere nodes.
- Does AWQ/GPTQ internal micro-ops mix cause branch mispredictions on some kernels? We saw hints in the sampled stacks but need deeper kernel instrumentation.
- Is there a cost tradeoff threshold where routing to a slightly slower median but stable kernel is net-better for customer SLA? Need cost-model integration to quantify.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing the microburst replay
- capture producer trace: use local traffic recorder to capture request seq lengths and KV outcomes for a 2-minute window from prod-shadow.
- replay harness: use bench-replay with preserved timing jitter and seed control.
- profiler config: CUPTI sampling at 10k events/s, nvprof L2 and DRAM counters, collect serveflow per-request tags.
- metrics: tokens/sec (median/p95/p99), kernel_switch_rate, sm_efficiency, DRAM bytes, enqueue-to-complete latency.

Closing note
This diary is intentionally rough. The behaviour here is subtle and probably why it escaped our usual steady-state battery. The fingerprint idea seems promising — it gives a quick binary classification we can use in the scheduler and in release gating for new quant profiles. Will update as follow-ups land.

-- Marcus
